title: How long they waited to go public
caption:
Airbnb waited 12 years to go public. Amazon waited 3.

We lined up 10 giants by the gap between the year they were founded and the year they listed. The four founded after 2000 (Facebook, Airbnb, Uber, Snowflake) took 8 to 12 years. The four founded in the 1990s (Nvidia, Amazon, Netflix, Google) took 3 to 6.

Microsoft is the outlier from the ’70s: 11 years, from 1975 to its 1986 IPO.

Which number surprised you most?

title: In 2008, cereal kept Airbnb alive
caption:
In 2008, cereal kept Airbnb alive.

Out of cash and with investors uninterested, the founders designed two election-themed cereals, Obama O’s and Cap’n McCain’s, and sold the boxes for $40 each. They made about $30,000.

The boxes did something better than pay the bills: they won over Paul Graham, who had doubts about the idea itself. Y Combinator invested $20,000 for 6% in January 2009.

Save this for the next time someone says you need funding to start.

Sources: Fortune (2023), UChicago Polsky Center (2021)

title: Will cheaper AI mean more AI? The Jevons paradox
caption:
Will cheaper AI mean more AI?

In 1865, economist William Stanley Jevons argued that more efficient steam engines wouldn’t save Britain’s coal. Cheaper power would invite new uses, and total coal use would climb. That idea is now called the Jevons paradox.

It came roaring back in January 2025, when Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella cited it the day DeepSeek’s low-cost model shook AI stocks.

Economists add a caveat: efficiency usually produces a partial rebound in demand, not a full backfire.

Sources: NPR Planet Money (2025), Fortune (Jan 27, 2025), Northeastern University (2025)

title: Microsoft’s first product was sold before it existed
caption:
Microsoft’s first product was sold before it existed.

In early 1975, Bill Gates and Paul Allen told MITS, maker of the Altair 8800, that they had BASIC software for its new computer. They didn’t. With no Altair of their own, they wrote it on a simulator Allen built on Harvard’s PDP-10, with Monte Davidoff writing the math routines.

Allen wrote the last missing piece, the loader, on the plane to the demo. It worked, MITS licensed it, and Microsoft was officially founded on April 4, 1975.

Sources: Computer History Museum, The New Stack, Wikipedia (Altair BASIC)

title: This week in 1992: the first text message
caption:
34 years ago this week, someone sent the first text message. It said “Merry Christmas.”

On Dec 3, 1992, Neil Papworth, a 22-year-old engineer at Sema Group, typed it on a computer and sent it over Vodafone’s network to director Richard Jarvis, who was at the company holiday party.

Jarvis’s phone, an Orbitel 901, weighed about 2.1 kg and had no way to type a reply.

title: Dropbox started with a forgotten USB drive
caption:
Dropbox started with a forgotten USB drive.

On a bus from Boston to New York, Drew Houston realized he’d left his thumb drive behind, again. He started writing code to make the problem go away.

Syncing was hard to explain, so he made demo videos. The March 2008 one, stuffed with in-jokes for Digg readers, took the beta waitlist from 5,000 to 75,000 overnight.

title: The Bitter Lesson, explained
caption:
The bitter lesson, in one swipe.

In 2019, AI researcher Rich Sutton looked back across seven decades of AI research and saw one pattern: methods that simply scale with more computing power keep beating methods that encode human expertise.

His examples: chess, where massive search beat Kasparov in 1997; Go, about two decades later; and speech and vision, where learning beat hand-built rules.

Sutton later shared the 2024 Turing Award with Andrew Barto for their work on reinforcement learning.

Sources: Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson (2019); Wikipedia

title: Spanx started with $5,000 and a pair of scissors
caption:
Spanx started with $5,000 and a pair of scissors.

title: Your org chart ships with your product: Conway’s law
caption:
Your org chart ships with your product.

In 1967, programmer Melvin Conway argued that the systems an organization builds end up mirroring how its people communicate. Harvard Business Review rejected the paper. Datamation published it in 1968, and Fred Brooks later named the idea Conway’s law.

Teams that don’t talk build parts that don’t fit.

title: Networks grow by squares: Metcalfe’s law
caption:
Why do networks get more valuable as they grow?

Around 1980, Ethernet co-inventor Bob Metcalfe sketched a simple idea: the possible connections in a network grow roughly with the square of its users. Two users share one link. Twelve can form 66.

His real point was critical mass. A network has to get big enough to be worth what it costs.

George Gilder named it Metcalfe’s law in 1993. Critics say the true curve is flatter, since not every connection is equally valuable. Metcalfe later received the 2022 Turing Award for Ethernet.

Sources: IEEE Spectrum (2006), Wikipedia

title: James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes
caption:
James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes.

Starting in 1979, frustrated by vacuums that lost suction, he built cyclone after cyclone in a shed behind his house. By his count, 5,126 failed. Manufacturers wouldn’t license the idea, so he licensed it in Japan and used the income to start his own company.

The DC01 launched in the UK in 1993 and became the country’s best-selling vacuum within about two years.

title: This week in 1947: the transistor’s first demo
caption:
This week in 1947, the transistor got its first demo.

At Bell Labs in December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed two gold contacts onto a sliver of germanium and amplified a signal up to 100 times. On Dec 23, they showed Bell Labs leadership.

AT&T then licensed the transistor to other companies for a $25,000 advance against royalties. Bardeen, Brattain and William Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Sources: Computer History Museum, IEEE ETHW
